utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Shall we have the appearances the today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis and Aditya Menon, assisted by our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, colleagues from the OTP, everybody in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson representing the Defence of General Delic, with assistants Lana Deljkic and Asja Zujo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So Mr. Berbic, at the beginning of your testimony yesterday, you made a declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. I remind you that you are still bound by that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, there's one point I want to clarify. During your testimony yesterday, you indicated you became the head of a segment of the Security Administration which is located at the Kakanj command post and that you believe that this had occurred in October of 1995. Can you clarify which segment of the Security Administration in Kakanj you were responsible for?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the segment for staff security affairs. But as I was the head of that segment, I was also responsible for the work of the other staff belonging to other segments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when you say "other segments," can you refer to the formal title of those segments?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, yesterday, the representative of the first department; we, from the second department, a couple of us people; and one person from the section for military police affairs. That was more or less the segment that I was answerable for in terms of organisational work and discipline --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- over those two or three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit P02834.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you see the document in front of you, Mr. Berbic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if we could have the whole English document on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you see the document in front of you, Mr. Berbic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: What's the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the 17th of December, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And to whom is this document addressed?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is addressed to precisely this segment of the Military Security Service at the Kakanj command post, to me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you -- after the section where it's addressed to you personally, there's an instruction there. Can you carefully read that instruction to yourself? Have you had a chance to read that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are here at Bulletin 237 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Just read it -- have you read it to yourself?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you saying whether I had received this document and had read it then?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: No, no, now. I just wanted to make sure that you were familiar with the contents of that statement, because I was going to put a question to you. Have you had a chance to look at it right now and to read it and to familiarise yourself with it?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This content under the word "Bulletin," I did not read, and nor did I familiarise myself with that part of the text, this complete text, other than the word "Bulletin." I just familiarised myself with the instructions given here in the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you comply with that instruction that was -- that's set out in this document when you received it in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember, but I probably must have complied with it if I was there, because I didn't have to be there at all times. If I had been there, I would have certainly complied with these instructions and submitted the document to whomever I was to submit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you explain how you would have gone about complying with this instruction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objections, Your Honour. The witness said, "I don't remember," and he gave a hypothetical response. And the question was, "How did you act to comply with the instructions?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, to the extent that the witness can recall how he would comply with such instructions when he actually received them, I think that he can give an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm still trying to read the witness's previous answer. I think I'll allow the question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, if you could please indicate how you would comply with the instructions set out in this document.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you with precision what the procedure was; and specifically about this case, I can't tell you because I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, you don't remember whether you did or did not comply with this instruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not remember the details in either case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the details. I'm just asking you: Did you comply with the instruction that is given up here, before the writing that is under the "Bulletin"? Did you comply with the instructions, or do you remember whether you did or did not comply with the instruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not remember specifically, in regard of this number, whether I complied or did not comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 365.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit P02835.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. To whom is this document addressed?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is addressed to the Kakanj command post, the Military Security Service, and then to me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And there's an instruction there from General Jusuf Jasarevic to you. Did you comply with that instruction?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot recall whether I complied with this specific instruction, according to this particular document, because that was 12 years ago, but I don't think that there were any reasons for me not to have complied with it and act according to the instruction. But specifically, in regards to this particular document, I cannot remember whether I really did. That day, I might not at all have been there. I might not have been at work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Berbic, when you -- when you do recall receiving instructions from Mr. Jasarevic, would you, in those cases, generally comply with those instructions?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes, I would comply with instructions, provided, however, that I did not look at the bulletin or at the content of the bulletin, nor did I need to look at them. I would simply place everything in an envelope and take it to the DC or some of my staff would take it to the DC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And in your absence, was there a procedure in place for such documents to be delivered to the DC?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a procedure. I do not see the time of receipt of this document. Perhaps if there was one, I could explain better because this particular document arrived via the Communications Centre, and then there was no signature. Perhaps if I could see the very top of the document. Well, we can see here that the document arrived after 1800 hours. In such cases, the person on duty in the segment of the administration of the Military Security Service at the Kakanj command post would receive this or such a document from the Communications Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what was the person on duty supposed to do with the document when they received it?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person on duty would wait for the following day, when I'd arrive, and would hand over that document to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And then what would you do with that document?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would look at the instructions in the document. I would put it in an envelope and submit it to the most responsible person at that point in time at the DC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berbic. Your Honour, I would ask if this document could be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 366.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit P02839.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: To whom is this document addressed?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is addressed to the command post at Kakanj, the Military Security Service, to me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And from whom are you receiving this document? Who's the -- from whom is this document coming from?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document came from the administration -- from the administration of the Military Security Service, from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Who signed the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can the witness see the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It's actually in the middle section. It's in the middle part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying the document is signed in the middle, Mr. Menon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, the sender of the document, the person who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But you're asking the witness who signed it. He must see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, actually, Your Honour, it's a typewritten signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, this is a document that's addressed to you. Which person is addressing this document to you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which person. The initials indicating who wrote the document, who authored it, actually do not match the name of the person who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And who signed the document, then?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have a specific situation here. I see no signature, which in fact is quite normal because the document was received by radio packet communications, so that I cannot know who signed it. Actually, I can just read what it says here by way of signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: In this document, are you being instructed to do something?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Who's giving you -- who is giving you that instruction?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signature says "Head, Brigadier General Jusuf Jasarevic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, I would ask that this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 367.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit P03059, and it's actually page 39 of that exhibit. It's a fairly lengthy exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It's actually 39 of the English as well, if we could go to 39 of the English and the B/C/S. I only see both English versions on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what's the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 27th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And who is this document addressed to?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is addressed to the command post in Kakanj, the Military Security Service, to me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if you could look at the first paragraph, there's instructions.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Did you comply with those instructions?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot recall, because this is a critical date, in fact. I'm not quite sure whether I was on duty on that day. It is quite early on. Apart from that, given the signature that we can see on this document, I fail to see how I could have received this document at all, I mean, in what way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If you could look at the handwritten notation on the left side of the document, can you just look at that? It's at the bottom of the document, on the bottom left-hand side of the document, Mr. Berbic.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Would the sender or the receiver of that document, of the document in front of you, have made that notation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who would have made the notation, the sender or the receiver?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'm putting the question to the witness so he can testify to it.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who affixed this notation there. But if you're asking me who generally could have done it, and as far as I can make out, what is written here is: "Went on the 28th of September, 1995," or "went out." That probably refers to the document having gone out at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, would the sender or the receiver of this document have made that notation? I'm not looking for a specific person, just for you to identify whether it would be the sender or the receiver that would have made this notation.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on. If you could look at the second paragraph in this document. Did you comply with that instruction?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the specific case, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'm talking about -- it's worded in a very general way, Mr. Berbic, and so I'm speaking generally. When you had this responsibility, when you were receiving these bulletins personally from Mr. Jasarevic, would you comply with the instruction that's set out in the second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would, of course, seek to comply with the instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And how would you comply with those instructions?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an instruction that arrived to the effect that on familiarisation with this document, the document was to be returned to the segment of the Military Security Service at the Kakanj command post and to be kept in custody, in a safe place, meaning safe or some other safe place where all the other documents were being kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you elaborate upon what that safe place was, since it was you that was charged with this responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That place would be an iron cabinet, for instance, the key to which was held by the two of us who worked on staff security affairs. The steel cabinet was in our room, and no one else was actually supposed to handle it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And so who was the other person that you're referring to, because you said "the two of us"?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I was the man in charge, which is to say in the period from October to the end of December, or perhaps January of the following year, the staff occupying that position changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon, how much longer are you going to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'm just about ready to finish up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask if this document -- just this page of this exhibit, if it could be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Menon, could you just explain to us what we are trying to establish with these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: With this document, specifically, or with the other documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think they have almost the same line of evidentiary importance, because they're all dealing with the task of the witness to bring something to the attention of somebody else, and I'm curious to know, the sender, as I recall in all cases, were General Jasarevic, and I suppose -- or maybe we would ask the witness where was General Jasarevic located, situated, when these messages were sent. Secondly, to whom is the witness asked to bring these documents? And so as to better understand the importance and significance of these two or three documents that you've shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'll put those questions to the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, you heard the questions posed by Judge Harhoff. Where was Mr. Jasarevic based when these documents were being sent?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot state where he personally was; however, his seat, his office was supposed to be in Sarajevo. Of course, occasionally, he moved about the free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And to -- and to whom were you supposed to bring these documents?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would take these documents to the DC. I didn't have to wait for anyone in particular. I would simply deliver them to the most responsible person there at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The instruction, if I may, the instruction is that the document should be brought to the army General Staff commander. Is that the same person as the DC?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, you've heard the question from the Judge. Is there a distinction between the DC, which, yesterday, you referred to that as the Distribution Centre, and the army Staff commander? Is there a distinction between those two?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the DC yesterday, and I have the same thing in mind today. There were those offices there that I mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And whose offices are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the offices of General Delic and General Hadzihasanovic, as well as the offices of some officers from the Operations Administration. There was some other offices, such as the protocol and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me for pursuing this, but the interest, of course, is whether General Delic ever received these documents. I mean, if you were asked to - I'm asking the witness now directly, if I may - if you were asked to bring these documents to General Delic, then you say that what you did was rather to give it to the Distribution Centre, and then let someone from that centre bring it to General Delic. Is that how it worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, in other words, you did normally not bring the document directly into the hands of General Delic, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If he was there at the moment, I was supposed to deliver it to him. If he was absent, I would give it to General Hadzihasanovic, who was the Chief of Staff. If he was absent as well, I would deliver that to the highest-ranking officer of the Operations Administration. There is a document in existence which regulates the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. And, so, if General Delic or General Hadzihasanovic were not immediately present at the moment you came up, then you would give it to somebody else, instructing that person then to bring it to the addressee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you then subsequently verify if actually Delic -- General Delic or General Hadzihasanovic ever received the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was duty-bound to check, but only to the extent whether they were familiarised with the document. Someone from the service would give me a call. They would tell me that has been done and that I can come and pick up the document. I suppose that General Hadzihasanovic, on occasion, would familiar himself with the documents, thus completing the task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. So we can assume that the documents that were intended to be brought to the knowledge of General Delic or General Hadzihasanovic were actually brought to their knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot say that for certain. If General Delic was absent, he may have been told about a certain document through General Hadzihasanovic. It was up to them as to how they organised that. General Delic was there very seldom and would stay for only a short while. This is what I know from taking the documents there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I'm a bit confused now. Yesterday, Witness, I understood that you stated that "DC" meant the place where several offices were located, among others, the office of the General Command, and that it was not only the Distribution Centre that was located there. And did I understand that "DC" meant all that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I can explain, Your Honour. The Distribution Centre was the name of the company that was there until the war. It was the name of the facility. In the facility, there was no distribution centre, nothing of that sort. However, on the first floor, there were still some offices of the distribution centre, which subsequently were used for the needs of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In those offices, General Delic, General Hadzihasanovic, some Operations Administration officers, as well as the protocol people were. There were some seven or eight offices in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Actually, I was still --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I was just going to finish up with the witness, Your Honour. It will be another four minutes, at the most. I would first ask if this exhibit, I think it's still on the screen, if it could be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Just this page, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought it was given Exhibit number 368.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. May the document please be given an exhibit number, as it has been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 368.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, for how long were you based at the command post in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was based at the Kakanj command post as of the moment I was sent to serve with the Military Security Administration, or rather, it's segment at the Kakanj command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when did you leave the command post?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the command post, together with the entire service, I believe in February, although I'm not quite certain. In February 1996, we went to Sarajevo. Once the Dayton Accords were signed, we started packing up. There was no reason for us to stay there, since communication was now free. It was open.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when did you leave the administration of the Military Security Service?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon my arrival in Sarajevo, in the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina - I believe that is the correct name - I asked in writing to be sent to another administration. I left in February or March 1996; in any case, at the beginning of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berbic. The Prosecution has no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Menon. Just before I hand you over to Madam Vidovic, you were asked how long you were based at the command post in Kakanj, and you said you were based at the Kakanj command post as of the moment you were sent to serve in the Military Security Administration. Can you give us a date as to when you were sent to serve at the Military Security Administration, because you don't seem to have answered that question completely; at least, I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will try to be as precise as I can. I believe I joined the service in July 1994, and I stayed with it until February or March 1996. It all had to do with the Dayton Accords; and after that, I left the service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Berbic. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and I will cross-examine you today on behalf of General Delic. Given the nature of cross-examination, you will be able to answer simply "yes" or "no" to many of my questions. If there is any need for clarification, I will ask you to provide it, or you may be asked questions by the Judges. I will do my utmost to complete your evidence today, and, therefore, I would kindly ask you to be as brief as possible when giving answers. We speak the same language; therefore, please allow a short pause between my question and the beginning of your answer, so as to allow the transcript and the interpreters to catch up. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, you completed the Air Force Technical Academy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed the Air Force Technical High School, which is lower than the Air Force Academy.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the former JNA, you worked with communications. Communications is your specialty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you remember that you provided a statement to the investigators. Do you recall that? To the investigators of the OTP, on the 16th of September, 2005; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to remind you of that statement and to ask you about a part of it which I deem of importance for this case. During 1992, you worked on the establishment of communication links in Visoko; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the former JNA, during its withdrawal from certain parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where non-Serbs lived, took away or destroyed most of the equipment that it had?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I could access quality information, given the function I had, I can tell you that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They destroyed the relay hubs which were supposed to relay information, and I just wanted to mention a few. The one at Vlasic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Donje Mostre?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At Zlatiste?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At Vraca near Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And some others. I believe you will recall that.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And also Hum, just above Sarajevo, the relay hub there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that during 1993, in your evidence, in your testimony here, that there was radio communication in place. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that there was a lot of improvising when trying to secure communication links?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You communicated with Sarajevo by telephone, for example, while you were still at Visoko?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a telephone line to Sarajevo from Visoko until August, I believe, August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that, that link was disrupted. All telephone communication around Sarajevo ceased?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The central cable that connected Zenica and Sarajevo was cut off, severed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, at a certain point in time, certain bodies of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina received satellite telephones?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw a device like that. We had one of those at Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it was a very open, unprotected way of communicating?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the communications system, that link is the most vulnerable, and it is the last resort to be used in dire need.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, it was not very favourable to convey military information and sensitive information; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, to conclude with this topic, I wanted to ask you this. Perhaps you can tell me if I'm right. It would be fair to say, wouldn't it, that communication links with Sarajevo, generally speaking, throughout 1992/1993 were very difficult, difficult to use?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the entire war, including those situations when packet communication was used that you mentioned today, since you mentioned encryption, would you agree with me that there was often a disruption, a breakup, of such communication links?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such communication was often interrupted since a signal could be scrambled or interfered with. It also depended on the number of repeaters that the Army of the Republic of B and H managed to put up, which was in very few places given the situation in the theatre; therefore, that type of communication was also very vulnerable. The very principle and use of packet communication is actually that was taken over from the Ham radio operators in the US. It's a civilian way of communicating.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As regards that, I wanted to ask you this: When there is a document that was signed, an original document, which says "Sent," is it correct that we can never be sure that the document that was sent actually arrived anywhere?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When talking about the end of 19 -- well, the person who would send such a document from the Communications Centre in Sarajevo would have to have some sort of confirmation that the document was indeed received. Those were the rules within the communications branch.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand correctly that that person would have to make a note that he was actually advised that someone received the document on the other end?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person receiving has a protocol, a procedure of his own. He would have to note down when and what document he received. The sender on the other side also needs to know what is it that he sent and whether it was received. I'm only talking about communication between communication centres.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I had in mind, too. We can ascertain that a document was sent, provided it was registered with the receiver; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And if it was noted down in the protocol forms; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berbic. I want to move on to another topic. Yesterday, in your testimony, you said that, in 1994, you began working at the command post of the Staff of the Supreme Command at Kakanj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like the witness to see Exhibit 280. It is an order for the Supreme Command Staff to be relocated, dated the 2nd of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please take a look at page 1, and now look at this date here. Do you agree that you know that this command post functioned from the beginning of 1994?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: "Order for the Staff of the Supreme Command to go out to the command post, the 2nd of January, 1994."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is an order for going out, relocating.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me just ask you this: When you started working at that command post, when you arrived at it, you found there the Brigadier Asim Djambasovic there as the head of the Operations Centre of the army, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you also found the Staff of the Army there?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the witness please also take a look at page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the document, please, and do you agree that the administrations which are listed here, as well as their segments, were also functioning at Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document can be put away, and now I should like Exhibit number 281 to be shown to the witness, please. For the record, this is a document which is entitled "Organisation of the Deployment of the Staff of the Supreme Command." It is an order of the 16th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, will you be so kind as to look at item 1 under the word "Order." It is not very clear, I'm afraid, but please do your best. Yes, I think now you can see that part. Witness, would you please look at item 1. It is true, is it not, that the Staff of the Army worked in Kakanj according to establishment, when you started working there?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, the Operations Centre for planning, preparation, organisation, monitoring, and control of combat operations, according to establishment, was also working there at the time; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Will the witness now look at page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please look at 9, line 9. It refers to the "Department of the Military Security Service of the Security Administration of the Ministry of Defence." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just before we repeat, Madam Vidovic, the interpretation referred us to line 9. I don't know what you may have said. We're not able -- I'm not able to follow, in the English, what to look at. Is it line 9 or paragraph 9? I see the answer at paragraph 7 on this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in English, it is the fourth bullet which starts with: "Department of Military Security Service," and in the Bosnian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the Bosnian version, Witness, do you see, I believe it's in the ninth line, it says: "Department of Military Security Service of the Security Administration of the Ministry of Defence." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now please take a look at this same part. Do you agree that parts of the Administration for Personnel, Mobilisation, Legal, parts of the Administration for Moral Guidance, Logistics, and so on and so forth also worked there?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at item 3 now. It refers to control at the command post, at the Kakanj command post. Would you please be so kind as to read item 3 to yourself, not aloud, and then I will ask you a question in connection with it. In connection with it, I should like to ask you this: It is true, isn't it, that the work of the administration organs and of parts of the Staff of the Supreme Command which were located in Kakanj unfolded in accordance with the Staff plan under the direct control of the Chief of Staff Hadzihasanovic; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you saw this order, and I should like to ask you, in that connection, this: You arrived in the course of 1994 and stayed there up until a period after the Dayton Accords. Is it true that, in fact, the Staff of the Supreme Command, i.e., its segment in Kakanj, functioned in the way envisaged in this item 3 that you have just read? Did it evolve in practice in keeping with this order?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It did evolve in practice in keeping with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. As regards this question of control and command in Kakanj, I will be reverting to it later on; but at this point, I should like to ask you something about the service -- the Military Security Service, in view of what you saw in this bullet number 4 -- or rather, in the Bosnian line number 9 "Department of Military Security Service of the Security Administration." Mr. Berbic, I concluded from your testimony that during 1994 and 1995, namely, while you worked at Kakanj, you were a member of that particular service. Is my conclusion correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is true, is it not, that the Military Security Service, in the course of 1994, was actually comprised within the framework of the Ministry of Defence; am I correct? It was an integral part of the Ministry of Defence? I'm asking you. I'm not talking about your particular segment. I'm talking about the Military Security Service as a whole. The Military Security Service as a whole, did it function as part of the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it functioned within the framework of the Ministry of Defence, but I believe that later the Military Security Service came to be comprised within the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "later," is this 1994 or some period in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was already the period when I arrived or perhaps a bit later. I cannot recall exact exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In this connection, I should like the witness to consult 375 -- 385 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: D375.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D375. For the transcript, this is an excerpt from temporary establishment structure, number...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not catch the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... of the Ministry of Defence of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with Staff attached units. The number was T412.303, from March 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please take a look at page 2 of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown page 2 of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just before we move on to commenting on this document, please, for the needs of the Trial Chamber and all of us here, because we are not soldiers by profession, if I can put it that way, please be so kind as to clarify the following: Am I right if I take it that a temporary establishment structure is a document which actually prescribes the composition of a certain formation in war; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, parts of units are designated or parts or formations which are comprised within that unit; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Temporary formations apply until the time of the adoption of other, i.e., the prescription of new formations or establishment structures; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We are still on page 2 of this document. Do you see that this temporary formation document was signed by the Minister of Defence, Hamdija Hasanovic, on the 25th of March, 1994; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the date the document bears.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, if the witness can now move on to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, can you now take a look -- a closer look at this chart, and specifically look at the chart of the Ministry of Defence with headquarters, support units. Do you agree that we have the Presidency at the top, then the Government of the Federation, then the Ministry of Defence? And this connection, what does this mean where it says "General Staff" and "Commander," and this arrow pointing at it? Can you clarify for us? Thank you very much. I apologise. If you can be of assistance, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This line on the right means that they were in communication, that they were in contact. I don't know what concretely you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you talk of the line that points to "General Staff," I'm not with you, Madam Vidovic, and I understand that things are very faded here. I can't see very well. I may perhaps just not be seeing the words "General Staff" because I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Your Honours, I apologise. Perhaps I wasn't quite clear. Here you have a square on the right-hand side, where it is written "Commander"; and above it, in the English text, you have the words "GS," and in brackets, "Main Staff," "Main Staff." In fact, Your Honours, I never could tell my right hand from my left-hand side. I hope you understood me properly. Perhaps that is where I was confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's my problem, Madam Vidovic. I was just about to ask you, "to the right of the diagram or to my right?" Which right? To my left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So it is to the right. I hope that you can see it now. It is this part where it says the "Main Staff," just above the word "Commander."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I now know when you say "right," I must go left.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Well, it appears to be so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it being almost time for our break, perhaps we could go back to this document after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, before the break we discussed the organisational chart of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of B and H, with the headquarters, support units. There's the Ministry of Defence in the middle, then the minister. I am interested in the boxes below. Somewhere in the middle, do you see a box that reads "Security Administration"?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see it in the English, please. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you this: When this temporary establishment was in place during 1994, the Security Administration was subordinated to the Ministry of Defence; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps we can show the next page of the document to the witness, please. Very well. I believe the witness's assistance will be needed, since we will regularly encounter certain terms pertaining to the Security Administration throughout the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you mentioned the first, second, and third department. Do you agree with me that this is the organisational chart of the Security Administration? Yesterday, you mentioned a Department for Counterintelligence Affairs. You also mentioned the Department for Information analysis; is that correct? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the chart that I discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The last department, if I'm correct, is to the right-hand side. It is the Department for Staff and Security, Military Police Personnel, and Legal Affairs. Is that the part you testified about yesterday, when you said that you were a member of that department, that you personally worked for that department; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I worked in that department.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you what is the most relevant portion concerning this chart for me. A section of this department went to the Kakanj command post following the minister's decision; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that section went to the Kakanj command post, and it was operational there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To be more specific, that is the section for staff and security and military police affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that that section that was in Kakanj had close ties with the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. Its name describes and explains its link to the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the Kakanj command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, I wish to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 369.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I believe I am correct if I say that the organisation of life and work at the Kakanj command post was done in a way that -- in the way that it complied with the rules of service of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in accordance with the rules of service of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps we could show D377 to the witness. For the record, this is a document drafted at the General Staff at Kakanj, dated the 29th of March, 1995, on the organisation of life and work at the General Staff KM. It is an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, first and foremost, I would like to ask you whether you want to have a hard copy that I have here, since I am not sure you can read what's on the screen. I believe we will be able to read the relevant portion; however, if you encounter any difficulties, I do have a hard copy that I can offer. Please have a look at the document. Do you agree that in the title, it says "Organisation of Life and Work at the Command Post of the General Staff of the Army of B and H," and that it is an order?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says that this organisation has to do with organisation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: That this order ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation]... has to do with the organisation of life and work at the command post of the General Staff at the ARBH.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that the introductory portion of the order invokes the rules of service in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the portion at the beginning, it says: "Pursuant to the rules of service in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina," and in order to regulate the life and work at the KM GS ARBH.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, have a look at item 2, please. It says "Command and Control."

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will slowly read it. It says: "At a time when the commander is absent from the KM, the Chief of Staff ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just an explanation for your sake and the sake of the rest in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, first, tell us whether it is correct that the acronym "RIK" means "command and control" or "to command and control"; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the acronym means.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you've encountered it numerous times?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: "At a time when the commander is absent from the KM, the Chief of Staff of the ARBH exercises command and control; and at a time when both of them are absent, command and control shall be taken over by the officer holding the highest position or rank, or an officer assigned by a special order of the commander or the Chief of Staff. "The Chief of Staff shall exercise command and control by using military police through the administration organ at the command post. Post. The command and control headquarters administration should be exercised by the Operations Administration."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a look at the last page, page 4 of the document, so that the witness could see the signature there, and then I will resume my questions regarding the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the signature, Witness? Can you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is the signature of General Delic, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise it as General Delic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, for a certain period, including 1995, you worked in Kakanj, and you know how things functioned there. Is it correct that the command and control at the command post at Kakanj functioned exactly the way as regulated by this order?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. Yes, it functioned in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 370.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you provided answers to the Prosecutor's questions, and you also replied to certain questions posed by Judge Harhoff today that had to do with General Delic and his stay in Kakanj. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember yesterday's questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, did I understand correctly that you basically today said that General Delic was seldom in Kakanj? Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I knew at the time and what I could see, based on that knowledge, he was in Kakanj seldom.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to remind you of the statement you gave to the OTP investigators. In it, and I would like to quote paragraph 83 of the statement dated the 16th of September, 2005, whereby you explained that he came when he would have to travel abroad or had some work to do in the area; is that correct? Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. As to whether he indeed went abroad, I cannot recall, but I think there were certain situations like that. He also toured other corps and units at the defence lines of the Army of the Republic of BH. So when he could go there or return from there, occasionally I would see him either at the Operations Centre for a short time or I would learn of his arrival at the KM.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How often, how frequent was it? Can you tell us how often or how seldom you saw him there?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say I saw him seldom, infrequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that he had his office in the DC facility. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: His cabinet, and I do not mean physically the office -- or rather, let me ask you this first: When he came there, he used the room you specified as being his office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about his cabinet and the personnel that worked with him. The members of his cabinet, they did not work there, did they?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of his cabinet did not work there, except for 1995, on several occasions, his secretary was there, or rather, she stayed at the motel. She had a room there, if that's what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, I meant his Chef de Cabinet. For instance, in 1995, it was Mr. Bulpasic. Did he used to work there or in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bulpasic did not work there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Zeljko Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zeljko Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was his associate.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Murat Softic, the former Chef de Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see Murat Softic there, either.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's correct, is it not, that his associates would pass by at the Kakanj command post?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they would come to the KM Kakanj, there would usually be a driver, an escort, the secretary. I don't know whether there was anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the General and his cabinet, and the colonel of the of the Staff of the Supreme Command, in principle stayed elsewhere, not in Kakanj; would that be a fair thing to say?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, tell us this: All activities that had to do with combat actions and operations actually took place at the command post in Kakanj; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, such activities would usually take place at the KM in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will move on to a different topic. Now, yesterday, you testified on the modus of reporting between the corps and the command post at Kakanj. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, I'd like to ask some questions of you that had to do with the role of the Kakanj command post in the process of reporting. First of all, I wanted to ask you this: Do you agree that there are rules in place -- that there were rules in place concerning the system of dissemination of information among units? You are aware of that, since you worked in communications; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were rules on the way of submitting reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The rule was for the lower unit to report to the first immediately superior unit; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the way it was, according to the rule of service, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, a battalion could not report to a corps, nor could a brigade report to the Supreme Command, provided it was not -- it had not been directly subordinated to it; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the command post of the Supreme Command Staff at Kakanj, therefore, received reports from the corps on events unfolding in their zones of responsibility; right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So they did not -- it did not receive reports, for instance, from divisions or brigades? From divisions or brigades.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not supposed to receive reports from divisions or brigades, according to the rule of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In fact, the corps command or the appropriate department compiled a report on what they considered to be essential for their zone of responsibility; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the manner of reporting between the corps and the command post of the Supreme Command Staff was regulated by an order? Was it the case? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was certainly regulated by an order but, of course, I cannot recall which one.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your Honours, can the witness please be now shown D378. Your Honours, I should like to explain. We are going to be using two documents as D378 which bear the same date, which is the 27th of December, 1994. Both are documents of the Supreme Command Staff, and they concern the regulation of the dispatching of reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you please first look at this page that you see before you. Would you agree that it says that it is a document of the Supreme Command Staff at the Kakanj command post, the date being the 27th of December, 1994?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that that is the heading and that that is the date on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And it concerns the sending of reports. It says "Report sending"?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say sent, addressed to all corps, inter alia. Witness, please bear with me and listen carefully. I'm going to read this order out for you. The first item says: "Corps commands and units in the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina shall, in future, send their combat reports exclusively to the KM in Kakanj. Combat reports from the corps which contain crucial changes on the BH front, positive or negative reports indicating problems under the jurisdiction of the General Staff commander, will be forwarded to the commander, wherever he may be at the moment, by the duty OC/Operations Centre." Please take a look at the signature which says "Deputy Commander."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that seems to be on the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: "Deputy Commander," and at the same time Chief of the Supreme Command Staff. The name which is typewritten is "Hadzihasanovic," but obviously someone signed in his stead. Are you familiar with that signature?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can not remember. It is written "Enver Hadzihasanovic," but I cannot really recall whether this is indeed his signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But let me ask you this in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does say "for" here?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said "for." Very well. Let us go on. It is true, is it not, that as of this date, which is the 27th of December, 1994, the corps commands dispatched combat reports exclusively to the Kakanj command post, and that is where you received them? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Yesterday, you testified about certain reports of the 3rd Corps sent to the Kakanj command post, did you not? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I read out some sentences from those reports and commented on those reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Witness, let us now take a look at page 2, the second portion of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page of this document, please. Your Honours, perhaps, this is a rather faded copy, so we shall give a hard copy to the witness of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, please take a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometimes, Your Honours, we have a problem with the scanning, and the copy which is produced is not as clear as the original document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, please, take a look at this document. Do we agree that it also bears the date the 27th December, that it also regulates the subject matter of the sending of reports, and that it is an order? You can gather as much from the document; right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Exactly. That is exactly what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will quote for you: "In order to secure the functioning of command and control and the necessary degree of protection and of security of information, I order: Summary combat reports from the Staff of the Army of the BiH will be delivered by the Administration for Operations Affairs via the Operations Centre in Sarajevo to the Presidency; to the commander of the General Staff of the Army when he is in Sarajevo; to the Main Logistics Centre, Visoko; and to the Administration for Morale for the purpose of informing the public." What -- the question that I want to put to you has to do with this: When the document says "will be delivered by the Administration for Operations Planning via the Operations Centre," summary reports will be delivered through them -- by them, that is. I should like to ask you about what you said yesterday when you said, "We would prepare these reports in sublimated form." What you actually meant is that you summarised the reports or you prepared summary reports. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this order was respected throughout 1995, was it not, as long as you worked there?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the way in which we worked through the Operations Centre -- this is the way we worked through the Operations Centre, as I also mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the commander of the Supreme Command Staff did not receive reports that arrived at the Kakanj command post from corps, but all the corps reports would be summarised, summaries prepared, and sent to Sarajevo, to the Presidency, and inter alia also to the commander; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. This document also states: "Deputy commander, at the same time, Chief of Staff Brigadier General Enver Hadzihasanovic"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you were aware of these functions of his, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was also regulated by the order; his function, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can these two documents be tendered under one number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The two documents are admitted under one number. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 371.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now I shall try to demonstrate what we have been discussing on an example of a document, so could you please put away these documents and show the witness the same exhibit that he saw yesterday, that was shown to him by the Prosecutor; that is, Exhibit 363. For the transcript, this is a document of the Command of the 3rd Corps of the 16th of June, 1995, which says "Regular Combat Report."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You read it yesterday, Witness; namely, that this report was sent to the General or Main Staff at the command post at Kakanj. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You looked at it yesterday. Please remember this date. I should like to direct your attention at this part where it says: "The situation and the activities of the enemy," where it refers to the Zavidovici --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Thank you. We would like Their Honours also to be able to see that portion of the document that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it says: "The situation and activities of the enemy," and you can see it refers to the Zavidovici-Mount Ozren axis and the Vranduk-Prnjavor and the Tesanj-De Venta axes. We are concerned with these two axes. Please focus on and remember one of these axis; for instance, this first one, the Zavidovici-Ozren axis under item 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page number 1 again, please, item 1?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look here under the Zavidovici-Ozren Mountain axis. There is a description of the aggressor's activities and the region of Jablanica is referred to, so please make a mental note of that. After that, look at the Vranduk-Prnjavor axis, which is on the next page in the English version, and look, for instance, at this. It says: "On the Vranduk-Prnjavor axis, the aggressor organised attacks from the direction of Kosovnjak and Balabanovac." Right. I'm just asking you to remember these locations that I'm referring to. Very well. Now, please look, again, at the portion shown to you yesterday by the Prosecutor, which is under item 2, item 2, which describes a situation and says: "The 35th Division." The last sentence says: "The next combat activities will be executed in which the El Mujahid Detachment will be participating."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for Theirs Honours, if the next page could be shown, because that particular portion is shown on the next page. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please make a mental note of this also, Witness. You remember commenting on this yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if this document can be now moved away, as I wish to show you another document. Can the witness please take a look at D385. This is a report. I apologise, Your Honours. Your Honours, I should just like to say at this point, as you are not going to have the entire document translated, that we really encounter serious problems with translations, which practically block me in my cross-examinations. So we are only able to have the most essential parts translated, and I do regret the fact that you cannot see these documents translated into English in their entirety. I shall certainly request that this document be completely translated, but, believe me, it is beyond my powers to do anything to improve the situation, and I am asking you to please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll bear with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours, for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Witness, this is a report of the General Staff of the Army, the Administration for Operations/Planning in Kakanj of the 17th of June, 1995. The document is entitled "Situation in the Theatre of War" for the 16th of June, 1995. Is that correct?
