Do you agree that it says that this memo is to be submitted to the president of the ARBiH Presidency and to the commander of the Army?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree that this is what it says. And next to the commander there's also the GLOC Command mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From this particular section, we can see that on the 17th of June, 1995, on that date, the General Staff of Army in Kakanj, through the Planning Administration, forwards information on the situation on the 16th of June, and the information is sent to these addressees. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They also state the commander -- they mention the commander of the army here; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall me showing you earlier today the document dated the 27th of December, which stipulated that the Operations/Planning Administration should be forwarding summary reports to Sarajevo, to both the Presidency and the commander? Do you recall that this was the case?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And as you see, this document confirms this, because it says the Operations/Planning Administration -- or rather the Administration for Operative Planning as the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And this is the way that things operated in practice; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The administration drafted the document and forwarded it to these addressees through the DC [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at page 2 of the document now?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let's have the top of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at this, and do you agree that the activities of the aggressor are being described there, and then the activities of our forces?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree. This is in compliance with the standard procedure governing these reports and their particular headlines.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at page 3 of the document now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the part where the signature can be seen in the Bosnian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that we can see that the document was drafted by the head of the Duty Service, Ibrahim Begic? Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He drafted the report. I know the person, and he has passed away.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But at the time, he was working there?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 1 on our screens once more. Your Honours, can we just correct a mistake on the transcript. On page 47, line 1 -- or rather, the previous line, line 25, my question was: "In what way did things operate in practice?" The witness said: "The administration drafted the document and forwarded it to the addressees," and the witness said "through the Operations Centre" and not "through the Distribution Centre." If we could clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was it the Operations Centre?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. The report went through the Operations Centre, where there was the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This mistake was on page 47, line 1; instead of -- or rather, the "DC" was recorded instead of the "OC," "Operations Centre," if this could be rectified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam. I guess it has been rectified.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, look at page 1 and tell me if you agree that what this describes are the aggressor's activities. I wish to draw your attention to the last sentence of the document. You see here, in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, which is relevant to our case, and that's why my question has to do with that. Do you agree --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, I'm referring to the lower bottom part of the document, beneath the headline "Aggressor's Activities." There should be a body of text following that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, it says here that the aggressor acted against places and so on and so forth. You see that the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps is being described here; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This has to do with the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 2 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the section of the document where the 35th Division is being described. In the beginning, they're describing the activities of the 35th Division in their area of responsibility in the Ozren part of the theatre. Heightened movement was noted in the area of the Jablanica village. Do you recall me mentioning certain locations in the report of the 3rd Corps? Is it true that the 16th of June report concerning the 3rd Corps dealt with this particular part of the theatre?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The mentioning of Jablanica in that other report?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the mention of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And please look at the section where they're mentioning the Vranduk-Prnjavor axis, where they're saying that the aggressor carried out infantry attacks from Kosovnjak and Balabanovac towards the Pribije sector. Do you recall these localities being mentioned in the 16th of June report of the 3rd Corps that I just referred to a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I recall that. I recall the location of Balabanovac that has been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at the text that follows further down, concerning the "Activities of our Forces." Do you agree that it is the first time that the 2nd and 3rd Corps are being mentioned, at the very bottom of the document, where it says: "In the area of responsibility of the 3rd, 4th, and 7th Corps, our forces responded occasionally to the provocations by the aggressor." In doing that, the firing positions of the aggressor were noted, as well as their fortifying positions and coordinating fire. Please look further down, where it says "Casualties" or"Losses."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be scrolled up, please, so we can see the bottom part of it, and can we have the following page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Losses concerning the 2nd and 3rd Corps, we can only see "1 TR." That's for the 2nd Corps, and there were "2 TR" and "3 LR" for the 3rd Corps. I suppose that "TR" and "LR" stand for severely or lightly wounded. Would you agree with me, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please go carefully through the document now. Before I put my question, let's go back to what we said. We said that "LR" stood for "Lightly Wounded" and "TR" for "Severely Wounded." I thought you agreed with me on that point.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've just seen the 16th of June report that the 3rd Corps had sent to the Kakanj General Staff. You saw that there was a piece of information concerning the El Mujahedin Detachment there?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that, quite simply, the piece of information dated the 16th of June went from Kakanj to Sarajevo, to the commander and Presidency, and that this piece of information has simply disappeared when it comes to this summary report from Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This summary report does not contain that piece of information which had been sent to Sarajevo. It has been left out.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it was left out simply because this was a lower-ranking unit which did not bear any significance for the strategic level of the army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officer who drafted the report decided on whether to include that piece of information or not. He was experienced enough to do that job. The level of a detachment would not normally be included in such reports, unless there were some radical situations involved. Therefore, my answer to your question would be, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify this. A radical situation would involve some unusual and highly-significant events or security problems, and only such a piece of information would then be sent on to the commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be assigned an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 372.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we set this document aside now. I want the witness to look at another combat report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just ask you a question, because I thought that the purpose of showing us these documents was to give us examples of documents submitted through the witness, some of which would go only to the command post in Kakanj, while others would be so important that they would be forwarded directly to the Main Staff. If this is correctly understood, then my question is: Which of these documents would then only go to Kakanj and which of them would be so important as to be forwarded directly to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, quite respectfully, it seems to me that this was not my intention. Yesterday, the Prosecutor showed a report to the witness which was sent from the 3rd Corps to the Kakanj command post. The witness testified that out of this extensive report and several other different reports arriving in Kakanj, a summary report was made. I have just shown what the summary report was like, with the intention of showing what sort of information reached the commander in Sarajevo, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I find this helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome, Your Honour. I will be dealing with the other sort of documents that the Prosecutor had been dealing with, by all means. Could the witness be shown document P22 -- or rather P02272. This is a regular combat report dated the 20th of July, 1995. It was also made by the 3rd Corps and was sent to the Kakanj command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please have a good look at the document once it appears on the screen. Bear the date in mind. Do you agree with me that this is the 3rd Corps Command report dated the 20th of July, 1995, and addressed to Kakanj? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you see, the document speaks of the situation and the activities of the enemy, UN forces, and UNMO. Look at the axes involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now be shown, one by one, the second, third and fourth pages of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Take a good look, please. You see the situation and activities of the 3rd Corps are being described here at the top of page 2; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if you can see it in the English version. Yes, Your Honours, now you can see the situation in the 3rd Corps. Further down, the combat morale situation is described. Now you can see it. Can we have the next page, both versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You see, Witness, the mobilisation and organisation-related issues, reinforcement, the logistic support. And at the bottom, you see, added in handwriting, "the security situation." This was added in handwriting by someone?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let's have a look at the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You see there: "State of security, security situation." I believe you were able to view this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now if we can have a look at the last page, where the signature is, and Their Honours can see it as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It says "Commander." "Colonel Ekrem Alihodzic, on behalf of the Commander." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to ask for an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 373.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic, how much longer are you going to be? According to the time calculation, you're left with two minutes compared to what the Prosecution used.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think half an hour. I believe that this is sensitive subject matter and that we would require more time than allocated for me to be able to make you understand the matters discussed clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, perhaps I failed to mention something. In the previous document, I think there was a mention of the El Mujahedin Detachment. I omitted this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps we can have the document back on the screen. I don't know whether it is -- it has been exhibited. I think it is 373. Perhaps we can have a look at the second page one more time. Exhibit 373, second page, please. Page 2, please. Perhaps it is on the next page, where it says "Situation and Activities." The next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please focus on the part which says -- look at the paragraph which says there was a regrouping of forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was a regrouping of forces. It says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Perhaps counsel could specify which paragraph she was reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Counsel, you're asked by the interpreters to specify where you're reading from.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I was reading from the second page, under the title "Situation and Activities of the Forces of the 3rd Corps," the third paragraph. It is marked now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: "Redeployment of the 4th Manoeuvre Battalion, forces from the 1st Corps zone of responsibility to the 35th Division. Zone of responsibility is completed in the village of Cardak with the purpose of joining the El Mujahedin Detachment." Witness, please bear that in mind. This is the report sent by the corps the KM Kakanj on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can put this document away now and show another document to the witness, D379. For the transcript, this is a Command Post Kakanj document dated the 21st of July, 1995, with the title "Situation in the Bosnia-Herzegovina Theatre" for the 20th of July, 1995. This document is to be distributed to the army commander and the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, Witness, that this is what it says, that this is a General Staff document from Kakanj, the 21st of July? Below that, it says: "Situation in the BH theatre on the 20th of July, 1995"; and among others, the commander is one of the addressees. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the introductory portion. Do you agree with me that it says: "Based on daily combat reports of corps commands," and so on and so forth. This is the situation on the BH front on the 20th of July, 1995; can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The subtitle says: "Activities of the Aggressor" on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move on to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, have a look at "The Activities of Our Forces." Do you agree with me that these are activities of the units of the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Corps that were described here? Do you agree that the activities of all corps on the 20th of July were described on this single page?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now move on to page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we scroll the English down, please. Can we see the top of the page. Thank you. Can we keep going. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at page 2 again. No, the third page, in the middle. In the English as well. The second page of the English, please. Please let us see where it says the 3rd Corps. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, have a look at the text where it says "the 3rd Corps" out loud. Not out loud, sorry. Read it to yourself. It literally takes up the space of only five lines, if I'm correct, six perhaps.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are five lines of text.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, we saw the reports for the 20th of July, 1995, that was sent from the 3rd Corps to the command post of the General Staff in Kakanj. It had four pages, if you recall. Now, those four pages become five lines of text in this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that there is no mention here of the El Mujahedin unit in this part of the text that has to do with the activities of the 3rd Corps? Please have a careful look.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can see, there is no such mention. There is no mention of that detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this an example of the summary reports you sent after having received corps reports at the command post in Kakanj? You would send such reports to the Presidency and General Delic in Sarajevo. Is this an example of such a summary report?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It contains all of the items that needed to be reported on. That is how I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this confirm what you told us before, and that was that the units of small size, such as companies and detachments, would not make it into such a report unless there was a specific reason?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would not, unless some drastic situations had to be mentioned, completely extraordinary situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have an exhibit number for this document, and I believe it is time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 374.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, we stopped at those summary reports. I would like you to give us another clarification. I was showing to you reports from the 3rd Corps that had arrived at the command post of the Staff in Kakanj, and then reports that were sent from Kakanj to Sarajevo, to the Presidency or the commander; right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this connection, I should like to ask you whether it is also correct that all other corps dispatched such reports; namely, reports on daily combat activities which they sent to Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, or the other corps and the GLOC, which is the main logistic centre, also did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, such summary report was to comprise all the information that had arrived at the Kakanj command post from all the corps. It was to be, as you put it, "sublimated" and then submitted to Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I do not have much time on my hands to show you a lot of other documents, but I should like to remind you that the Prosecutor showed you, yesterday, Exhibit 361. This was a daily combat report of the 3rd Corps of the 8th of October, 1994. Do you remember that? A report from 1994 was shown to you.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will remind you. There was also a report from the 3rd Corps from the 3rd of April, 1995. This was Exhibit 362. I would remind you, in both these reports, you read out for our benefit portions which dealt with information on the El Mujahedin Detachment, sent from the 3rd Corps to the Kakanj command post. Do you remember them now?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I do. Yes. They were shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you can in no way confirm for us that that information from the -- were actually sent from the Kakanj Staff, Supreme Command Staff, to General Delic, can you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I do know is that such information was comprised within a joint report in the Operations Centre in Kakanj, and then that report would be submitted to the known addresses in Sarajevo, the commander and the others. I'm not aware of any other ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we would have to consult those reports to see what exactly had gone to Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards these reports, you actually don't know anything; and when I say "these reports," I'm referring to the reports of the 3rd Corps which contained information about the El Mujahid, the ones that you read yesterday, namely. So you personally don't know anything about the accuracy of the information that was written in those reports?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. That information was received in the form of reports, which I neither verified nor needed to check out. I simply participated sometimes in the compiling of a joint report, in respect of the elements which pertained to the security item.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Berbic, I shall now like to ask you a different thing, because you are one of the rare witnesses who could appear before this Tribunal and who has actually worked both on security duties, while at the same time being a communications expert. Therefore, I will ask you to clarify some of the things which figure very often here, in terms of contents of documents and their manner of transmission.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can the witness be shown at this point D380.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, may I ask you to slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. I will do so, and I apologise. D380, Your Honours, this is a document which consists of three sub-documents, which are interlinked, as you will see.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I should like you to look at this document of the General Staff of the Army. Do you see the date, which is the 22nd of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you can see that this is about -- that the General Staff document is submitted to the Security Administration. That appears to be the case. Can you tell us what this is actually about?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about, namely, this report, judging by its heading is a consolidated, sublimated report about the successes of the combatants of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 21st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should just like us to see the signature. The second page, please, of both the English and the Bosnian versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the name written here "Deputy Chief in the SVB, Colonel Sacir Arnautovic," and you knew this person, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is true, is it not, that General Jasarevic was this person's superior at the time this document was made? Right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go back to the first page of this document. Can you please scroll down the English version a bit. Please focus on the fifth paragraph in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document refers to -- take a look at the fifth paragraph. It refers to certain successes. I'm interested in the last sentence, which says: "Fifty bodies of dead Chetniks were pulled out to our side, while about 40 were captured alive by the El Mujahedin unit." Please make a mental note, Witness, of this information, and now take a look at the top of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The very top. Please scroll down the English version as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, this is of the essence. This question that you refer to in your statement today, and this is a question which might be sowing confusion amongst people who are not versed in communications and military structures; namely, today you said that documents were transmitted via cryptographic protection. And as you are a specialist in signals, in communications, and as you obviously know what that is, would you please be so kind, Witness, as to explain to us what that means? What does it mean that a document is conveyed via cryptographic protection? What happens to the original of the document when it is being dispatched in this way?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it is conveyed under cryptographic protection, the document which is actually being transmitted remains with the sender. The original remains with the sender.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the document that is received by the recipient is a retyped document, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It came to the recipient by electronic means and is just simply printed at the recipient point by the printer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So that means when a document is transmitted under cryptographic protection, as is the case here, as is written here, so when it is transmitted in this way, it is not possible to see the signature. It is possible to see the name of the person where there is an indication of the signature; is that not right? Actually, you, yourself, drew our attention to that today.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is impossible to transmit the signature except by facsimile, and this was not the case here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now turn to the next page, Your Honours. Actually, I apologise, Your Honours, the third page of this document, the third page of the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please look at this document. You saw this memo of information with the same date, the 22nd of July, 1995. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall our reading this part, which is a bit lower, in the version in our language?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. It is the following page in English, so that I'm going to pause for a while. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So do you remember that we saw this bit of information about 50 dead bodies having been pulled out and then a tank was seized and so on and so forth? Do you remember that actually here there is no reference to the 40 people captured by the El Mujahid Detachment, which was referred to in the previous document? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document, that particular reference is not made. That bit of information is not contained in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So in this document, where the place for the signature is, it is written "Army General Rasim Delic"; do you agree? His name is indicated there?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, his name and his position.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that we have some initials here?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you agree -- would you agree that, thus, on the basis of just a document of this kind we just named, we're actually never able to ascertain for a fact whether that particular person did, indeed, sign the document if it was transmitted under cryptographic protection. Am I right? We would have to see the original?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have to see the original if an encoded document was sent in this way. What would be received would be only what the product of the printer would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please consult all these references here about all the corps, the successfully operations. Take a look at this text for a while. Now please look at the following page, the next page of this document in both our language and English.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please scroll down. Scroll down the Bosnian version for the witness to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you agree that this is a memo with the same number, the same date, exactly the same document as the one that we just saw, but the signature here --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see again, please, the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see here a "KZ" which actually indicates cryptographic date of protection, and indicates the exact time when it was dispatched, 14.48 hours, 22nd July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, please take a hard look at this signature. Do you agree with me that it was not actually signed by General Delic? A while ago, you said that you were familiar with his signature.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree. And apart from that, there is a "for" here which only confirms that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Right. So could you tell me if you perhaps happen to know who signed this? Are you familiar with this signature, if you can recognise it?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure in this form, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this document be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, once again, in order for us to be able to ascertain whether someone has signed an original document which is being sent under cryptographic data protection, we must be able to see the original; right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any document, every document which is transmitted under this "KZ" system has to be signed in the first place in order to be sent at all. That was the rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But in order for us to be able to know who actually did the signing, we would have to see the original; right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We would have to see the original in the file, in the protocol, to extract the actual document to see who affixed their signature to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, a couple of lines before, you asked that this document be admitted into evidence. Do you think you can allow us to do that? Before we do that, can I find out from the witness if he does recognise the signature of the person, the signature on the left, not the author, but the one who's signed under the cryptographic data protection thing, "1448 hours."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I cannot recognise that signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 375.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can put this document aside now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When preparing for your testimony, you were shown a large document by the Prosecutor. Its number is P03035, and they used portions of that document today.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was 3059.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to ask you something concerning the bulletins and special information. I do not mean the contents of any given bulletin, but rather about bulletins and special information in general, since you also worked in the Security Administration. I wanted to ask you this: Such bulletins and documents containing special information are actually documents by the Security Administration that were produced in a limited number of copies. Its addressees were clearly prescribed. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the documents of the Security Service, with a limited number of copies produced, each of which had to be filed and sent to a particular address.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the Security Administration issued an order on distributing such documents?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a standard procedure in place. I personally do not remember seeing such a document, but there was a procedure. Such a document was probably in existence; however, I do not remember it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please show D319 to the witness now -- 219. For the record, it is a document by the Supreme Command Staff, Security Administration, dated the 22nd of July, 1993, signed by Chief Jusuf Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, it is a short document. It says "Order," and then: "Bulletins and special information documents shall be prepared in five copies and sent as follows. Do you agree with me that the number of copies and addressees are clearly stipulated here?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by what I can see here, there were five copies, with their addressees from 1 to 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with me that the Security Administration bulletins or bulletin was intended -- or rather, the copy intended for the commander would arrive at Kakanj, that particular copy, I mean?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that copy would come to the commander in Kakanj and in Sarajevo, if he was in Sarajevo at the time or somewhere else. That's what I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is what you believe, then, but we're not talking about two such copies, but only one copy?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. I believe it was in October of 2005. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember describing in detail the procedure used with the bulletins?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is paragraph 52 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I wanted to ask you this: Do you remember having said that you would deliver the bulletin personally to the Chief of Staff, of course, in those situations when General Delic was absent?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I said that if he was absent, I would hand it over to the Chief of Staff or to the next highest-ranking officer of the administration. I believe it was regulated in such a way that it could be done with certain documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So that means that you wouldn't wait for Delic to come within a fortnight or a month and then to show him that, would you, or did you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I would simply take it there when I was told to and hand it over.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff, as you said, since you saw Hadzihasanovic's signatures on the documents, the Chief of Staff was at the same time the commander's deputy when he was absent?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We concluded that based on the organisational orders you've shown me today.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, I am correct in believing that when the commander was absent, bulletins would be received by the Chief of Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the commander was absent, the Chief of Staff would receive those.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I want to remind you of another part of your statement. That is paragraph 59, where you say that he would study the bulletins; and if he deemed it necessary, he would undertake certain measures. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember having said that; however, that is my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we opened up this topic and during your testimony yesterday and this morning, the Prosecutor showed you some documents concerning the bulletins, and you told us you would take them to the DC. In no way can you confirm to us whether they were actually delivered to General Delic, himself, am I correct, personally to him, or whether they ended up with Hadzihasanovic? Do you know any -- do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember any situations in which I delivered that personally to them. That was not the procedure. There was always the commander's secretary there, and I couldn't get to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you don't know whether Delic ever saw any of the bulletins, be it in Sarajevo or elsewhere, or whether his Chef de Cabinet saw it? You can't assist us on that, can you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything of the sort. I never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 376.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic, you have used 42 of the 30 minutes that you had asked for.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is a lot of documents and paperwork. I don't know whether this is -- whether we've given an exhibit number to this last document. We did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have, 376. But the point I was making is that you had asked for 30 minutes before the break, and we are now 33 minutes after the break, and you had used 20 earlier before we went for the break -- ten, rather. Do sit down.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that, Your Honour. I apologise. I moved along rather slowly since we had to refer to many documents; however, I do conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say you are done with your cross-examination, Madam?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination, Mr. Menon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Excuse me. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could pull up Exhibit P03059. If we could go to page 113 of the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Where is the document being sent?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was sent to the command post of the General Staff at Kakanj, Military Security Administration, for General -- Colonel Sacir Arnautovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what does the document instruct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is an instruction to the effect that the Military Security Administration is forwarding this particular bulletin dated the 24th of June, 1995, so that it could be delivered to the commander of the General Staff of the Army, Army General Rasim Delic, for his information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in this document, which should be page 112, English and B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Is this document also being sent to Kakanj, and does it also instruct Mr. Arnautovic to forward a bulletin to General Delic, along with a document entitled "SI"?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document reads sending bulletins to the command post of the General Staff of the Army at Kakanj, the same address. The instruction is that it should be forwarded to the General Staff army commander for his information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go to the next page of this document, both in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, does this document -- is this document also being sent to Kakanj, and does it also instruct Colonel Arnautovic to forward a bulletin and a special report to General Delic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to clarify something. The original is not sent, of course. This original remained in Sarajevo; however, probably it was sent to Kakanj via cryptographic protection, sent to this address.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Mr. Berbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could now go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that clarification confuses me. What do you mean by "the original remained in Sarajevo; however..." The original of what? Of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The original of this document, I suppose, since I see a handwritten note, "Sent on the 25th of June" at a certain time. It is a standard notation if a document is being sent by packet communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that mean that this is the original or that this is the copy that is retained by the author; whereas, the original that encloses these documents has gone to the recipient?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This original remained with the sender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the sender never sends the original; the sender sends the copy, is that your testimony, and keeps the original?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that communication means cannot forward a signature. They can only send or receive text. The contents of this were received at a certain address; however, the original remains with the sender, in this case the Military Security Administration in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would just note for the record that the last three documents that I showed the witness, two of them are dated the 25th of June, and then the first one was dated the 24th of June. If we could now move to page 110 of this exhibit, English and B/C/S, and this document is dated the 26th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, is this document also being sent to Kakanj, to Colonel Arnautovic, and does it also require that the bulletin be forwarded to General Delic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the addressee is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berbic. If we could go to page 109 of this document, English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Menon. Are you going to be going through a whole number of pages that say exactly the same thing as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I actually did intend to do that, and I feel it's necessary to do that for clarification, because on cross-examination this witness had indicated that General Delic was seldom in Kakanj. This exhibit contains a number of documents stretching from the end of June until the end of December, and they're all in a similar format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you're going to take us through all of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, to the point -- in order to make a particular point. I don't need to, actually. I'm prepared to tender this exhibit for that purpose at this point, but I expect that there would be an objection to that, so I'll sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when responding to the Prosecutor's questions, the witness said that General Delic was seldom in Kakanj. If it was his intention to prove that, I believe that the witness, this morning, the witness said that he was in Kakanj seldom. Therefore, I merely followed that up in my cross-examination. But the Prosecutor should have dealt with this during examination-in-chief, in that case. These documents should have been shown to him then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Perhaps, if I may interrupt, because I had the same question on my mind, how often General Delic was actually in Kakanj. And I noticed the witness's answer very specifically, because the witness said he seldomly saw General Delic in Kakanj. So I was confused, and I was going to put that same question to the witness afterwards, but maybe the Prosecution can clarify if the witness actually knew how frequently General Delic visited Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I can do that, Your Honour, and I certainly -- well, first, let me address the point raised by Defence counsel. I don't -- I certainly didn't put the question to the witness this morning as to how frequent General Delic was in -- was in Kakanj, and perhaps I'm wrong, but I don't recall the witness explicitly saying that General Delic was seldom in Kakanj. I didn't raise an objection when the question was posed simply because I thought that I would follow up -- follow it up on re-examination in this manner. I believe these documents speak for themselves. These are documents that are consistently being sent to Kakanj, requiring that material be forwarded to General Delic. And as I mentioned, they stretch across a particular period. And so certainly that was my intention, in going through these documents, was to illustrate that point. I can certainly put it to the witness, how frequent General Delic was in Kakanj, but I thought the best way to establish that point was through these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Menon. Yes. I think the witness clearly testified that he seldomly saw General Delic at Kakanj, as I said. This, of course, does not necessarily imply that General Delic was not there. However, the witness also testified that even when General Delic was in Kakanj, he would frequently just stop by and be there for a short period of time and then move on to somewhere else, perhaps touring the front lines or doing something else. So I'm not sure that the mere fact that a number of documents were sent to Kakanj, to be brought to General Delic, necessarily implies that he was there at all times. So let's be careful about what we're asking the witness to provide us with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I take Your Honour's point, and I can certainly move on, if that's the position of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No. It is not the position of the Chamber. The Chamber -- my position, at least, is that I wish to elicit from the witness his knowledge about how frequent General Delic actually visited Kakanj, not how often he saw him, but how often, to his knowledge, if he knows, he was actually physically present in Kakanj, and for how long he would stay there normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, to your knowledge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This whole discussion confuses me further. I was dealing with a specific point of being taken through, page by page, a number of documents which say the same thing, and I wanted to try and speed up the proceedings by suggesting, depending on the position of the Defence, that if you have a batch of those documents that say the same thing, and we have seen several of them already, which establish some kind of pattern, can't you just then tender them all as a batch into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I can certainly do that, Your Honour, and as I mentioned, I'd be prepared to do that right now, but I wasn't sure how many documents I would need to go through before I would be able to do that, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I notice my colleague on my left shakes her head. Maybe there is some mistake I'm making somewhere. Judge Lattanzi, would you like to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm rather confused, even more confused now. I understood that the Prosecutor was showing us all these documents not to establish a pattern that would appear, but simply to show us the dates of these documents and to highlight how frequently, how often General Delic was in Kakanj. Am I mistaken or was this your purpose, Mr. Menon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: That was my purpose. It was simply to show, I suppose, by implication, that if documents marked "Immediate" are consistently being sent to a particular location for a particular person, it might imply that that person is in that location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But isn't that establishing a pattern also?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Isn't that also establishing the pattern?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It's the same thing. I think it's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Look, I'll withdraw what I was saying. Just go ahead and conduct your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would ask now that this batch of documents, Exhibit P0359, be tendered into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This P0359 has already been admitted into evidence as Exhibit 368, but it is just the one page. I don't know whether you now want to tender the remaining pages as a separate exhibit, with a cross-reference to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's hear what --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we do not object to entering or admitting the pages shown by the Prosecutor today. As for the rest, as for the documents we didn't see, we are against that. We have nothing against admitting the documents that were shown to the witness, but only that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As I said to you earlier, Mr. Menon, I withdraw what I raised. Go ahead and prosecute your case. If you have to show us those page by page, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. Actually, I lost track of the page. I believe I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You were on 109.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I was on 109. Okay. Brilliant.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is no need to show all of the documents. If this will save court time, then we can admit it as such. I will withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would express my appreciation to the Defence for that, and I would ask that this now be tendered in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like to express my exasperation. You know, just go ahead. Go ahead, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask now that this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And now I'll pose the questions that Judge Harhoff --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 377.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: -- that I would ask that I pose to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Berbic, and I'm not speaking about how often you saw General Delic in Kakanj, but based upon -- based upon your knowledge, outside of how often you actually saw him, how frequently was he in Kakanj, based upon what you knew?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should just like to draw attention to the fact that, for instance, at the period from which these documents hail, I was a lower-ranking member of the Military Security Service, and my ambit of work did not require of me to have any direct contacts with Commander Delic. So let me repeat, according to what I knew, General Delic came to Kakanj only very seldom; and when he did come, he stayed there only for short periods of time. I had occasion to hear several times that he was there, or I would be told to submit something and I would go there and he would not be there. May I add something else, by your leave? I mentioned earlier that I saw him at two important meetings - of that, I'm certain - and perhaps another couple of times in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you for that interjection, Mr. Berbic. The Prosecution has no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Menon. Judge Lattanzi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have a question about telephone communications. You told us that at one point in time telephone communications through land lines were cut off, and you were provided with a satellite communication system. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These communications were intercepted. There was also a lot of interference on the line. So it was very difficult to communicate, using this channel. So I would like to know the following: After the -- once the tunnel, the Sarajevo tunnel, was built, was the regular -- were the regular land lines back to work -- back at work?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't remember. I cannot associate the existence of the tunnel with the existence of communication links. But what I can say is, as far as I remember in 1995, I believe that there were regular telephone lines in existence. However, they were only used as a means whereby to send cryptographic reports; namely, in open conversations, the telephone was not considered a safe way of communication, and whoever wished to protect their information did not resort much to that particular way of transmitting information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more thing about these reports. You told us that you received reports from units who were on the field, engaged in combat, and that you would prepare summary reports, a compilation of all these reports, and it was only the summary report that was sent to the General Staff. But during the cross-examination, it seemed that we found out that these summaries were extremely brief and short, and you told us that you only included what you deemed necessary to be included in those summary reports; therefore, that you did not deal with all the matters in the summary report. So in the summary, we can't -- there were not elements of everything that had been sent by the corps. You only put the most essential elements in these summary reports; right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise. I'm not quite clear what it is that you want to elicit from me. I'm not quite clear about what the final question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask this question again. I'll reformulate my question. You told us that you were in charge of making summaries of these reports, and I wanted to know whether in those summary reports, you had had -- all the issues were covered, even in a very brief fashion, or whether you were allowed or you had the competence to decide not to cover certain topics that had been dealt with in the reports coming from the corps.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will briefly explain the entire procedure. All the reports from all the corps would come to the Operations Centre at the Kakanj command post. There, a team of people comprising members of all the administrations, among whom also I, myself, but not always exclusively I, it could have been one of my colleagues, would come together and everybody would deal with their part of the report. I dealt with the part of the report entitled "Situation of Security in the Units." It was my task, and I had the scope to summarise everything in five or six sentences, everything which concerned security and had come -- all the security information that had come from all the other units, three or four or five pages. It was simpler than to put together -- this was simpler to do than put together all those reports and send them as such to Sarajevo. So we extracted what we needed from those reports on the basis of our experience. It was at the discretion of the specialist assigned to that particular chapter in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the issues of security, for example, that's fine. So, to your knowledge, a topic regarding security, what was it? For example, the fact that units in the field would have behaved irregularly, something that you would have been told about in a report, and that you would have summed up in a summary report; would that be included, for example?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do apologise again. I'm not quite sure what it is that you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you told us that you were in charge of summing up topics regarding security. Among these questions regarding security, according to you, do you think that regular conduct on the battlefield, would that be included in those topics or not?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Yes, quite clear. This is my answer: From this multitude of pieces of information that we received daily and which were more or less similar every day, only if something happened out of the ordinary or, as I put it, drastic things, and if this was written in the corps report, for instance, if it was written that, for example, 50 members of some of the units of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for their personal reasons, disgruntlement or something like that, left the positions, the line of defence, without leave, that would be a great problem and that would have to have been reported; namely, included in the report that we sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, an irregular conduct towards the civilians or prisoners of war was not considered as an important topic that would be included in the summary report?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know what conduct that would be, but I have given an example which is important. There could have been incidents between civilians and members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina where the military police would intervene. If this exceeded some normal limits, then reports would be sent, but we did not want to burden the addressees with less significant matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Let me just ask for some clarification of the issue of General Delic's visits to Kakanj, because you said that, to your knowledge, he was rarely there.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. Could you say how many times that would be in 1994?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am unable to say that in respect of 1994, because it was July, the end of July 1994, when I arrived at the Kakanj command post. And in that particular period, July 1994, or rather, until the end of 1994, I saw him once or twice. I cannot remember exactly now. There were two important meetings. I saw them -- him then. That I know. And I could guess, but I don't want to do that. It was really a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That is perfectly fine. But, you see, we are sitting back with something we do not quite understand, and I would like you to help us understand, if you can. And what we do not understand is: Why would the Main Staff in Sarajevo send documents to Kakanj to be brought to General Delic if he wasn't there? How would you suggest that we understand these facts? Do you have an explanation? If you don't have, then please say that you can't explain that. But if you know why documents would be sent to Kakanj, even if Delic was somewhere else, then we would be happy to know.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would also have to guess why that was so. I was not in circles that were privy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I would rather just leave it at this, rather than having you speculate on something that you're not sure about. I have one other question for you, sir. If we could ask the Registrar to pull up Exhibit 369. And while we are waiting for that, let me explain a bit about my question, because I think I remember from the organogram that this exhibit includes, in your section, there was also -- there were two sections. There was one for military police affairs, in which you served, and then there was another section dealing with legal affairs. Let's have a look at the organogram, if we can find it. I thought it was Exhibit 369, but I might be wrong. If the parties can help me. It's coming up. Great. Now we have the organogram in front of us, but I am surprised to see that I can't find what I was looking for. I thought that there was, in your section, one department for military police affairs and another department for legal affairs. Maybe Ms. Vidovic can help me. Is it the next organogram? Can we move on to the next page, please? Right, there we are. Yes. If I understand it correctly, sir, you were working in the section for staff and security and military police affairs, and that was in the Department for Staff and Security, Military Police, Personnel and Legal Affairs. And on the organogram, just below your section, there was a section for personnel and legal affairs. Can you see that? Do you see it, Mr. Berbic? Yes. Now it's being highlighted in yellow for you.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, I do see the Department for Staff and Security Affairs and what it consists of, this section for staff and security and the section for personnel and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now, we are obviously interested in issues relating to the prosecution of crimes committed by members of the ABiH. So looking at this organogram, I am curious to know if you can tell us what was dealt with in the section for personnel and legal affairs. And to be more specific, my question is: Was that section dealing with prosecution of alleged crimes committed by members of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to tell you that this particular section was not at the Kakanj command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. So it was left in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know what they did in Sarajevo, what that section was doing in Sarajevo? If you don't, that's fine, just tell us so.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I would be able to tell you what a part of their duties -- a part of their work was, but I'm not familiar with the complete content of their work. I, perhaps, of all the staff that worked there, remember a couple of names. This was just a small section with just, for instance, three or four staff [is interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can you answer me very specifically on the question of whether, to your knowledge, this section was involved in the investigation and prosecution of crimes allegedly committed by member of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine with me. Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a correction of the transcript. Page 87, 1 and 2, the witness said that it was a small section with one or two staff, and what it says here is "three or four." So can this correction please be introduced there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope the correction is being made. It is quarter to. I have a few questions. I don't know whether the parties are going to have questions after this. I'm mindful of the fact that there is a desire for the witness to be released to go home. I don't know whether we can finish today. My questions won't take more than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And we have a hearing in this court at 2.15. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see if I can finish my questions. Sir, I'm going to try to be very brief. You have told us about a system of communication in your office in Kakanj and the rules that were being laid out for sending out communication. Did you, at every occasion, comply with the rules?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, personally, whenever I have that obligation, complied with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm asking about you; and if you can just say "yes," say "yes." And you carried out every instruction you were given?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as regards the sending of reports and that work, generally speaking, there existed rules which we sought to abide by. I can tell you that, but I cannot remember in every specific case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please let me interrupt. I'm not asking you about the rules. I'm asking you if you carried out your instructions as given. Can you remember an occasion when you did not carry out the instructions?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot remember one, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to say that, to the best of your knowledge, you carried out your instructions all the time?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we tried our best to carry out what was ordered us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Sorry, sir. I'm not asking you about all of you. I'm asking you about you, personally. My questions are centered on you, alone. To the best of your knowledge, did you carry out your instructions?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, to the best of my knowledge, I carried out the instructions given me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if instructions came on a day when you were not present, when you did come to the office, did you carry out those instructions that arrived in your absence?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I was not at the office or in the building, my obligations, at the time when I was the head of that segment, which is from October 1995, would be waiting for me in the morning, and I would discharge them then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I just want to follow on one question that was raised by Judge Lattanzi on the reporting of, as you said it yourself, drastic issues. If, for argument's sake, a crime was committed on the field, would you see that as a drastic measure to be reported in your drafting of the summary? I'm talking about you, personally.

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, had I received such information, had such information come in a report, I would have personally sought to incorporate it in the summary report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To your knowledge, in the whole office now - I'm now going beyond you - just the whole office, all of you who contributed to this report, would a situation like that be incorporated in the summary?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if such information was received from a subordinated unit of the corps, it would have had to be conveyed, but that depended on the people -- on the people who were on duty in the specific situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would the capture of enemy soldiers be seen as something worth putting in the summary?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in my opinion, if that involved a larger number, I would have incorporated it in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would a number of 40 be a larger number?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in my view, that would be such a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let me follow up on a question that was raised by Judge Harhoff. He asked you about the sending of documents from Sarajevo to Mr. Delic in Kakanj and was wondering why would he send that often if he wasn't there that often. My question to you is: Am I right to say you told us that Mr. Delic was, most of the time, at the DC in Sarajevo? That's where his main office was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Am I wrong? I guess the DC was not in Sarajevo; it was somewhere else. Where was it?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the DC building was in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry. But General Delic was based in Sarajevo. His main office was in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And he would undertake visits to the army, amongst others, to Kakanj, your office, like you say, you don't know how often?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, he would not come to where my office was because my office was on the other side, in another building, but I don't know how frequently he came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that, but the instructions that you used to receive to send these bulletins to Mr. Delic came from Mr. Jasarevic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, for a while, I was not in charge of this segment of the administration at the Kakanj command post, and I did not receive these directly from Mr. Jasarevic but from my immediate superior, Mr. Refik Cesko, who assigned this task --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you. The letters that were being shown here were drafted in the name of Mr. Jasarevic, am I right, which would say "For immediate action," that you must deliver the bulletins immediately? They came from him?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where was he based?

utterances.speaker: ENVER BERBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, General Jasarevic was based at the administration of the Military Security Service in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
